DEFENDANT’S MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO EXCLUDE PLAINTIFF’S EXPERT DR. SARAH D. KOWITT UNDER FED. RULE OF EVID. 702 Defendant JOpen, LLC (“Defendant” or “JOpen”) hereby files this Motion to Exclude Plaintiff’s Expert Witness Dr. Sarah D. Kowitt under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993) and incorporated memorandum of law. I. INTRODUCTION Plaintiff offers Dr. Kowitt as a purported expert on warnings to opine on the adequacy of Defendant’s warnings on the O.P.M.S. Silver kratom products, but her opinions do not satisfy Rule 702. They are not grounded in the governing Louisiana legal standard, not based on relevant scientific expertise, not based on any facts applicable to the products at issue, and not derived from any reliable methodology tied to the facts of this case. Under the Louisiana Products Liability Act, warning adequacy turns on what a manufacturer knew or, in light of then-existing scientific and technological knowledge, reasonably 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 15 could have known about a product’s risk profile at the time it left the manufacturer’s control. That inquiry is anchored in state-of-the-art science and regulatory context. The Court should exclude Kowitt’s testimony for multiple reasons. First, Kowitt has no regulatory, scientific, or medical expertise, and admitted that she has absolutely no knowledge about the contents or characteristics of Defendant’s kratom products. She therefore lacks relevant expertise to opine on the labeling requirements. Second, Kowitt’s opinions are not based on any legal or regulatory requirements, but rather mostly rely on an outdated textbook that discusses how to best communicate warnings with no actual application to the products at issue. All of Kowitt’s opinions are therefore improper and/or unreliable, confuse the issues, and would not assist the jury at trial. II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND A. Plaintiff’s claims and allegations. This is a products liability case in which Plaintiff alleges that O.P.M.S. Silver kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023. Specifically, Plaintiff claims that Defendant designed an inherently and unreasonably dangerous product, that Defendant failed to adequately warn of the dangers associated with O.P.M.S. Silver kratom, and that Defendant failed to provide adequate instructions on how to avoid such risks. See ECF No. 100, at ¶ 61; see also ECF No. 184 at 2 (Plaintiff brings a “products liability claims under Louisiana’s Products Liability Act, La. R.S. 9:2800.51, et seq., asserting that the kratom product consumed by Harmony [her daughter] was unreasonably dangerous due to a failure to warn and a design defect.”). B. Dr. Sarah D. Kowitt Kowitt is an Associate Professor in the School of Medicine at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and is an academic researcher on the psychology of communications Ex. 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 15 1, Expert Report of Sarah D Kowitt, PhD, at 1. Kowitt’s research focuses on how to best communicate warnings to consumers, how information is communicated, communication campaigns, and how consumers view and respond to warnings. Ex. 2, Excerpts from Kowitt Dep. 38:12–40:5, Feb. 18, 2026. Kowitt provided the following opinions with respect to the warning labels on the O.P.M.S. products at issue in this case: (1) “The Defendant’s warnings did not warn about risks associated with product use”; (2) “The Defendant’s warnings did not provide clear instructions on how to avoid risks associated with product use”; (3) “The Defendant’s warnings did not use language that was clear or understandable”; and (4) “The Defendant’s warnings’ format did not optimally capture or hold attention.” Ex. 1, at 2–5. III. ARGUMENT A. Standard for admissibility. The district court has considerable discretion to admit or exclude expert testimony under Fed. R. Evid. 702. See, Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 138–39 (1997); Seatrax, Inc. v. Sonbeck Int’l, Inc., 200 F.3d 358, 371 (5th Cir. 2000); Tajonera v. Black Elk Energy Offshore Operations, LLC, Civ. A. No. 13-0366, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8 (E.D. La. June 7, 2016) (Brown, J.) (citing authority). The burden rests with the party seeking to present the testimony to show that the requirements of Rule 702 are met. Moore v. Ashland Chemical, Inc. 151 F.3d 269, 276 (5th Cir. 1998). Rule 702 provides that an expert witness “qualified ... by knowledge, skill, experience, training or education may testify in the form of an opinion” when the following requirements are met: (a) The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 4 of 15 (c) The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Rule 702 codifies the Supreme Court’s opinion in Daubert, which charges district courts to act as “gatekeeper” when determining the admissibility of expert testimony. Tajonera, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8. The purpose of a Daubert motion is “to ensure that only reliable and relevant expert testimony is presented to the jury.” Rushing v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 185 F.3d 496, 506 (5th Cir. 1999) (superseded by rule on other grounds) (citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 590–93). On appeal, courts “review the admission or exclusion of expert testimony for an abuse of discretion.” Braggs v. BP Expl. & Prod., Inc., No. 23-30297, 2024 WL 863356, at *2 (5th Cir. Feb. 29, 2024) (quoting Huss v. Gayden, 571 F.3d 442, 452 (5th Cir. 2009)). Courts “will not find error unless the ruling is manifestly erroneous.” Guy v. Crown Equip. Corp., 394 F.3d 320, 325 (5th Cir. 2004). This provides courts with “wide latitude in determining the admissibility of expert testimony.” Watkins v. Telsmith, Inc., 121 F.3d 984, 988 (5th Cir. 1997). B. The Court should exclude Kowitt because her opinions are impermissible and offer no assistance to the jury. A court may exclude an expert’s testimony altogether if the opinions are substantially reliant on inappropriate legal opinions and lack factual support in the record, rendering the testimony fundamentally unreliable: [W]hile Daubert instructed that the focus of the reliability inquiry “must be solely on principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that they generate,” 509 U.S. at 595, 113 S.Ct. 2786, the Supreme Court later clarified that “conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct from one another,” Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 146, 118 S.Ct. 512, 139 L.Ed.2d 508 (1997). Thus, “a district court’s focus on principles and methodology need not completely pretermit judicial consideration of an expert’s conclusions,” Kuhn, 686 F.3d at 625 (internal quotation marks omitted), and a district court may exclude expert testimony if it finds “that there is simply too great an analytical gap between the data and the 4

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 15 opinion proffered,” Joiner, 522 U.S. at 146, 118 S.Ct. 512. Or, to put it in the language we have frequently used both before and after Daubert and Joiner, a district court may exclude an expert’s opinion if it is “so fundamentally unsupported” by its factual basis “that it can offer no assistance to the jury.” E.g., Loudermill v. Dow Chem. Co., 863 F.2d 566, 570 (8th Cir. 1988); United States v. Finch, 630 F.3d 1057, 1062 (8th Cir. 2011). In re Bair Hugger Forced Air Warming Devices Prods. Liab. Litig., 9 F.4th 768, 777–78 (8th Cir. 2021). If the factual basis of an expert’s opinion is so fundamentally unsupported because the expert fully relies on legal conclusions, altered facts and speculation, or fails to consider relevant facts in reaching a conclusion, the expert’s opinion can offer no assistance to the trier of fact, and is not admissible. E.g., Nebraska Plastics, Inc. v. Holland Colors Americas, Inc., 408 F.3d 410, 416–17 (8th Cir. 2005) (when opinion is “so fundamentally unsupported” in failure to consider relevant facts, it can offer no assistance to the trier of fact and must be excluded); McGlinchy v. Shell Chem. Co., 845 F.2d 802, 807 (9th Cir. 1988) (expert study and future testimony properly excluded where it rested on speculation, unsupported assumptions, and ignored distinctions crucial to arriving at a valid conclusion); Guillory v. Domtar Indus., Inc., 95 F.3d 1320, 1331 (5th Cir. 1996) (expert testimony properly excluded where it was not based upon facts in the record but on altered facts and speculation designed to bolster party’s position). 1. Kowitt is not qualified to testify as an expert regarding labeling requirements for kratom products. The Court should exclude Kowitt’s testimony in this case because she has no regulatory expertise regarding labeling requirements, and no scientific or medical expertise regarding kratom, and therefore lacks relevant expertise to opine on labeling requirements for kratom products. See generally Collett v. Weyerhaeuser, 512 F. Supp.3d 665, 674 (E.D. La. 2021) (excluding proposed experts where “there is no evidence to even suggest that either doctor has had any experience with the chemical involved in this case”). 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 15 Under the Louisiana Products Liability Act (“LPLA”), a failure-to-warn claim requires proof that the product possessed a potentially damage-causing characteristic and that the manufacturer failed to exercise reasonable care in warning of that characteristic. Stahl v. Novartis Pharm. Corp., 283 F.3d 254, 264 (5th Cir. 2002). Critically, Louisiana law defines that duty in terms of the “state of the art.” The LPLA provides a complete defense where, “at the time the product left his control, [the manufacturer] did not know and, in light of then-existing reasonably available scientific and technological knowledge, could not have known of the characteristic that caused the damage or the danger of such characteristic.” La. R.S. § 9:2800.59(B). A manufacturer must warn of dangers inherent in normal use that are not obvious, and “in performing this duty the manufacturer is held to the knowledge and skill of an expert and must keep abreast of scientific knowledge, discoveries and advances.” Short v. Otis Elevator Co., 502 So. 2d 1100, 1102–03 (La. Ct. App.), writ denied, 503 So. 2d 465 (La. 1987). Likewise, “[i]n performing this duty a manufacturer is held to the knowledge and skill of an expert; it must keep abreast of scientific knowledge, discoveries and advances and is presumed to know what is imparted thereby.” Weber v. Caterpillar Mach. Corp., 542 So. 2d 544, 551 (La. Ct. App.), writ denied, 548 So. 2d 332, 334 (La. 1989). Under this framework, evidence relevant to adequacy necessarily turns on what scientific and technical knowledge existed in the relevant field at the time the product left the manufacturer’s control. Any expert purporting to evaluate the adequacy of a warning must inherently possess expertise in the scientific and technical subject matter that defines the alleged risks. It depends on whether the manufacturer knew or, “in light of then-existing reasonably available scientific and technological knowledge, could not have known” of the alleged danger. La. R.S. § 9:2800.59(B). Thus, evaluating the adequacy of a kratom warning requires familiarity with kratom’s 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 15 pharmacology, toxicology, regulatory treatment, and the state of scientific knowledge regarding risks at the relevant time. Kowitt has none of that expertise. With regards to kratom itself prior to this case, Kowitt testified as follows: Q. Have you had any publications related to kratom? A. No. Q. When did you first learn about kratom? A. I don’t know for sure. Q. Was it prior to this case? A. I had a general awareness of kratom prior to this case. Q. Prior to this case, had you done any work related to kratom? A. No. Q. What level was your knowledge at about kratom? Was it sort of on the scale of “I’m kind of aware it exists” to “I’ve actually looked into this a bit”? A. I’m kind of aware it exists. Q. Had you possibly seen it for sale? A. Yeah, I’ve seen it for sale at gas stations. Q. Okay. Any knowledge beyond it was something that people might purchase? A. No. Ex. 2, at 14:23–15:18. Indeed Kowitt could not even confirm whether “the product at issue in this case was a synthetic product,” “whether it was created in a laboratory versus in a food product facility,” did not know “whether the product at issue in this case had 7-hydroxymitragynine in it,” and admitted she knew nothing “about the manufacturing of the product at issue in this case.” Id. at 65:10–66:13. In addition, Kowitt has never developed or drafted a warning label for any commercial product, nor has anyone ever retained her to do so. Id., at 123:2–11. She has not done so in this case either - she vaguely opines on things she believes the labels should include, but does not have an opinion on what she believes the warnings should actually say: Q. So what I’m struggling is we don’t know what the right label would look like according to your report. 7

Well, I gave descriptions of what an adequate warning needs to include, and that’s description of health risks, instructions for avoiding or mitigating those risks, and optimal design, clear, easy-to-understand language, readable – Q. Yeah, and those are abstractions; correct? A. I’m not sure what that means, “abstractions.” Q. Well, you give us some general guidelines of principles that should be in a warning; correct? A. Yes. Q. But we don’t have actually what the warning should be, as drafted by you? A. I did not provide an actual different product warning; correct. Ex. 2, at 93:11–94:2; see also id., at 20:17–22 (Kowitt did not “prepare an exhaustive list of what should be included in the warning label” nor was she “asked to develop what [she] thought would be an adequate warning label for kratom.”) And even if she had an opinion on an adequate label here, Kowitt testified that she “can’t say it would have changed [Harmony Moller’s] behavior in this case.” Id. at 92:15–17. As an example, Kowitt opines that the warning should have included a “pictorial warning” with images, analogizing the warnings on the O.P.M.S. products with the proposed, non-final “FDA pictorial cigarette warnings.” Id. at 84:13–15. Despite this “first of a kind” proposal for cigarette warnings, Kowitt couldn’t “recall any other examples of FDA requiring pictorial warnings” and had no knowledge of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act requiring pictorial warnings. Ex. 2, at 84:23–85:13. Nor could she, as there is absolutely no basis in any regulatory framework to include a pictorial warning, and indeed the FDA has never required any product in history to have pictorial warnings or graphics. Similarly, Kowitt recommended “ensuring that the warning is optimally conspicuous by using colors,” but likewise testified that she was not aware of any regulation requiring the use of colors. Id. at 84:16–18. She has absolutely no knowledge of the legal framework governing warnings. See id., at 16:24–17:1; 22:7–15; 80:13; 82:11–13. Moreover, Kowitt’s general experience in tobacco, cannabis and alcohol is insufficient and inapplicable here. Though Kowitt often analogized tobacco and cannabis warnings to those for 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 15 kratom products, such analogies are wildly off base, as Kowitt agreed that “cigarettes is one of the most heavily [regulated] consumer products in the market” and there have been “lots of developments in cigarette warning labels.” Id., at 29:22–30:9; 41:22–42:13. As such, her experience is not sufficiently specialized to the subject matter at hand, and courts frequently exclude experts who lack the specialized experience relevant to the issues in the litigation. Kowitt’s opinions and testimony will do nothing here other than confuse the jury, and this Court should exclude it. Louisiana law holds manufacturers to the “knowledge and skill of an expert” in the relevant scientific field. Short, 502 So. 2d at 1102–03; Weber, 542 So. 2d at 551. Kowitt is not an expert in the relevant scientific field. She cannot opine on what scientific knowledge about kratom existed, whether seizure risk was established, how it compared to other substances, or what risks were reasonably knowable at the time. Without that foundation, she cannot reliably assess whether Defendant exercised reasonable care in warning of kratom’s alleged risks. Courts routinely exclude experts who attempt to opine outside their field of specialized expertise. See, e.g., Rheinfrank v. Abbott Lab’ys, Inc., 680 F. App’x 369, 381 (6th Cir. 2017) (affirming limitation on regulatory and medical expert’s testimony on antiepileptic drugs, which was outside the scope of her expertise); Payne v. C.R. Bard, Inc., 606 F. App’x 940, 943 (11th Cir. 2015) (affirming exclusion of expert’s testimony on IVC filter, where expert has worked on one project involving an IVC filter more than twenty years ago, had never designed, tested, or manufactured an IVC filter, and had never taught seminars or published articles about IVC filters). Here, Kowitt’s general research experience in tobacco, cannabis, and alcohol warnings does not qualify her to opine on the adequacy of a kratom warning under Louisiana’s state-of-the- art standard. Because Louisiana law defines adequacy by reference to scientific and technological knowledge in the relevant field, and because Kowitt lacks that field-specific expertise, her 9

Kowitt’s opinions rest on a “best practices” analysis in outdated sources that are not based in science and will only serve to confuse the jury and prejudice Defendant. Plaintiff brings a failure to warn claim as part of her products liability action. “To successfully maintain a failure-to-warn claim under the LPLA, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the product in question has a potentially damage-causing characteristic and that the manufacturer failed to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning about this characteristic.” Stahl v. Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corp., 283 F.3d 254, 264 (5th Cir. 2002). Louisiana law expressly defines that duty in state-of-the-art terms. The statute further provides a complete defense where, at the time the product left the manufacturer’s control, the manufacturer did not know and could not have known—“in light of then-existing reasonably available scientific and technological knowledge”—of the alleged danger. La. R.S. § 9:2800.59(B). That legal framework makes clear that were an expert to be qualified to opine on the content of the warnings, that expert must possess expertise in the scientific and regulatory knowledge surrounding kratom at the relevant time. Kowitt has absolutely none. Kowitt, however, does not and cannot evaluate the body of peer-reviewed scientific literature concerning kratom and at the time of sale. She does not analyze or even possess any information about the regulatory treatment and waring of kratom by FDA, DEA, HHS, or other agencies. Nor does she or can she assess what a manufacturer exercising the “knowledge and skill of an expert” in the field could reasonably have known. Moreover, Kowitt seemingly, and improperly, conflates “best practices” with legal requirements for warnings, further emphasizing the need for preclusion. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 40 Opinions It is my opinion that the warnings on the kratom packages discovered near Ms. Moller were not adequate for the reasons outlined below. a. The Defendant’s warnings did not warn about risks associated with product use. Warnings are messages that communicate risks associated with product use to consumers. Warnings are necessary when risks associated with product use cannot be eliminated through product design.1 The purpose of warnings is to communicate important safety information, influence or modify people’s behavior to improve safety, and reduce or prevent health problems or personal injury.1 Warnings also enable potential consumers to make informed choices on whether to use the product.1 Warnings for products related to substance use generally contain three elements: 1) a marker or signal word (e.g., “WARNING”), 2) a description of the health risks associated with product use (i.e., description of the hazard and/or consequence), and 3) instructions for how to reduce or eliminate the health risk. Regarding the second element of warnings stated above, warnings should clearly communicate the health risks associated with product use and list specific health risks, rather than vague health concerns.2 The Defendant’s warnings stated that “ingesting Mitragyna Speciosa can be dangerous.” No specific health risks are mentioned, and the term “dangerous” is unclear (e.g., to whom is the product dangerous? Why is the product dangerous? What dangers may result from using the product? How serious are the potential dangers?) The Defendant’s warnings also state, “By opening this package you accept full responsibility for the use of the product including but not limited to any adverse events or health complications.” However, the warnings never state that adverse events or health complications could occur, nor do they specify what those might be. Rather, the warnings disclose that the manufacturer will not be responsible for any adverse events or health complications. This in itself is not a warning of health risks. The need to disclose health risks in the warnings was especially important given that the risks were serious and non-obvious. Research studies published before February 2023 (when the Decedent’s death occurred) show associations between kratom use and health risks that include but are not limited to substance use disorder, liver toxicity, seizures, cardiovascular effects, and death. For instance, Eggleston et al. conducted a retrospective review of kratom exposures reported to the National Poison Data System, published in 2019.3 Of 2,312 kratom exposures documented in their publication, 935 cases involved kratom as the only substance.3 Moreover, they note that “Kratom most commonly caused agitation (18.6%), tachycardia (16.9%), drowsiness (13.6%), vomiting (11.2%), and confusion (8.1%). Serious effects of seizure (6.1%), withdrawal (6.1%), hallucinations (4.8%), respiratory depression (2.8%), coma (2.3%), and cardiac or respiratory arrest (0.6%) were also reported.”3 Further, they note that “Kratom was listed as a cause or contributing factor in the death of four decedents identified by the county medical examiner’s office.”3 In addition, Kerrigan & Basiliere reviewed the origins, pharmacology, uses, and effects of kratom, published in April 2021. They noted several adverse effects associated with kratom, including “agitation, altered mental status, central nervous system depression, coma, confusion, dizziness, drowsiness/sedation, hallucinations, hepatoxicity, hypertension, irritability, nausea, respiratory arrest, restlessness, seizures, tachycardia, and vomiting.”4 While data and research on kratom continue to evolve, research conducted after the Decedent’s death in February 2023 continues to confirm that kratom is associated with adverse health risks. As of November 2025, 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 4 of 40 the FDA on its webpage on “the FDA and Kratom” notes, “FDA has warned consumers not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder (SUD). In rare cases, deaths have been associated with kratom use, as confirmed by a medical examiner or toxicology reports.”5 These research findings support the conclusion that there were known health risks associated with kratom use that the Defendant should have included in their warnings. Further, in his deposition as the corporate representative of Martian Sales, Mr. Mark Reilly stated he was aware in 2021/2022 that “kratom has been linked to, by the FDA, to adverse reports, including death and dependence” (page 54, lines 8-13). In addition, in his deposition (personal role), Mr. Mark Reilly agreed that warnings should “communicate to consumers any significant health risks associated with the use of the product” and should notify consumers “if there’s a risk of death for selling the product” (page 30, lines 8-23). b. The Defendant’s warnings did not provide clear instructions on how to avoid risks associated with product use. Regarding the third element of warnings stated above, warnings should provide clear instructions for ways to minimize risks associated with product use. The only instructions for use on the Defendant’s products were: 1) “consult your healthcare professional to determine if this product is right for you, and if so, how to use it safely” (disclosed under “directions”); 2) “Consult your physician about potential interactions, other possible complications, and precautionary measures before considering this product” (disclosed in the warning label); and 3) “Inform your physician of the alkaloid content, labeled on the package” (disclosed in the warning label). No information on the product package tells potential consumers how much of the product can be consumed and over what timeframe—both of which are basic requirements for product packaging and labeling. Moreover, the warnings do not provide information on how to avoid adverse effects, how to identify adverse effects (e.g., symptoms), or how to respond to adverse effects (e.g., contact information for a poison control center). The only stated instructions for use are to inform healthcare professionals. However, it is unlikely that healthcare professionals can advise consumers on kratom use, given that “No formal guidelines are available for treatment of kratom dependence or misuse, and only a paucity of evidence is available regarding long-term outcomes and success of treatment in primary care.”6 Moreover, while few studies have assessed healthcare professionals’ knowledge of kratom use, and those that have are limited by small sample sizes and a lack of generalizability, research shows potentially limited awareness and knowledge of kratom use by healthcare professionals. For instance, in a study of 257 pharmacists in Alabama, published in December 2023 by Penzak et al., 49.8% had not heard of kratom.7 Of the 50.2% who had heard of kratom, only “14% considered themselves knowledgeable or very knowledgeable about the herb.”7 In another study involving interviews with 12 public health and healthcare professionals, published in 2016 by Stogner et al., none had heard of kratom.8 Given that there are a variety of kratom products, it is also likely that healthcare professionals would not have been familiar with the specific product in question. In addition, the instructions to consult a healthcare professional provided on the Defendant’s products are not adequate to avoid or minimize risks associated with kratom use because research from nationally representative surveys shows that, in general, a majority of US adults do not disclose dietary supplement use to healthcare providers,9 nor do they have discussions with healthcare providers about substance use.10 In addition to not providing clear information on how to avoid risks associated with product use, the Defendant’s warnings contained unclear language regarding whether humans could 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 40 actually consume the product. Specifically, the warnings had statements that the product is “only for use as a botanical specimen” and that “Mitragyna Speciosa is an unapproved dietary ingredient.” If the product could indeed not be consumed by humans, then the warnings should have clearly and explicitly stated that humans should not consume the product. However, in his deposition as the corporate representative of Martian Sales, Mr. Mark Reilly agreed that this product is meant to be “consumed by humans” (page 88, lines 15-17), despite the products being labeled as “only for use as a botanical specimen.” Moreover, the advice to “consult your physician about potential interactions, other possible complications, and precautionary measures before considering this product” conflicts with the statement that the product is “only for use as a botanical specimen” because the only reason to consult a physician is if the product is meant to be consumed. Finally, including warning information in secondary locations, such as on a product website, is insufficient if the warning on the actual product package is inadequate.1 In other words, to be adequate, a warning should be placed directly on the product package because the product package is what consumers are most likely to see. Therefore, while the Defendant’s products stated in the disclaimer, “Please see full disclaimer at www.OPMSKratom.com,” and included additional information on health risks and dosing on the product website, because this information was not included on the actual product package, the Defendant’s warnings were not adequate in communicating risks or instructions to mitigate risks. c. The Defendant’s warnings did not use language that was clear or understandable. Warning adequacy is also evaluated by how warning content is communicated. In general, warnings should “use short, familiar words,” “use as little text as necessary to clearly convey the message,” “use short statements, rather than long complicated ones,” “use explicit language— tell exactly what the hazard is, what the consequences are, what to do or not do,” “use concrete rather than abstract wording,” and “use active voice rather than passive voice.”1 In addition, warnings should inform consumers about potential product risks using language that is at the lowest possible reading level and minimize the use of technical terminology.2 The Defendant’s warnings did not comply with these warning best practices in several ways. First, the Defendant’s warnings did not use short, familiar words; rather, the warnings used terms that included “botanical specimen,” “unapproved dietary ingredient,” “Mitragyna Speciosa,” and “alkaloid content.” These are technical, scientific, and/or regulatory terms that are not suitable for a general lay audience. Second, the Defendant’s warnings did not use as little text as necessary to convey the message clearly. Specifically, the Defendant’s warnings were 132 words long. Lengthy warnings introduce clutter, reduce readability, and make it difficult to discern risks associated with product use. Research shows that brief, concise, uncluttered warnings are more effective than those with clutter.11 In addition, the format of the warnings (all information listed in paragraph form using dense text) makes them more difficult to read and less effective at capturing and holding attention.1 Third, the average grade level of both warnings was 10.7 (measured using Flesh-Kincaid grade level). Ideally, warnings for the general population should be as low as feasible (ideally <8th grade level).1 Fourth, as mentioned above, the Defendant’s warnings did not use explicit or concrete language to communicate the risks (i.e., hazards and/or consequences) and instructions for avoiding the risks. These factors, especially when combined, support the conclusion that the Defendant’s warnings did not use language that was clear or understandable. d. The Defendant’s warnings’ format did not optimally capture or hold attention. 4

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 40 Finally, in order to effectively communicate product risks, warnings must first capture and hold attention.1 If warnings do not capture or hold attention, then they will not be able to effectively communicate risks or instruct consumers on how to avoid or minimize risks. Research shows that warnings increase attention by 1) including images or symbols (e.g., alert triangle symbol) and 2) using a conspicuous design (e.g., through the use of color, location, contrasting background, or other factors).1 To the first point, meta-analyses (which represent the strongest possible literature with the least bias) by Noar et al. and An et al. related to warnings for food products (sugar-sweetened beverages) and substance use products (tobacco) show that warnings that use images or symbols improve warning effectiveness on cognitive outcomes (e.g., thinking about product risks) and behavioral outcomes to avoid or minimize risks (e.g., increasing intentions to quit smoking, dissuading use of sugar-sweetened beverages).12,13 To the second point, in a meta-analysis of safety warnings, Hancock et al. found that conspicuous warnings defined as the “extent to which the warning stands out from its surroundings, either in terms of luminance, the use of bright colors, the use of contrasting background, or other factors which may make the warning more vivid and eye-catching” significantly improved warning recall.11 Similarly, in a meta-analysis of nutrition warnings and labels, Song et al. found that color-coded labels improved behavioral outcomes to avoid or minimize risks (e.g., nudging consumers’ purchasing behavior towards more healthful products).14 The Defendant’s warnings failed to comply with warning best practices to capture and/or hold attention since the warnings 1) did not use symbols or icons to increase attention and 2) were not optimally conspicuous (defined by a lack of color, placement of the warnings on the back of the packages, and the use of long, dense text to communicate information). While attention is not sufficient for determining whether a warning is adequate in and of itself, it is necessary to consider when determining warning adequacy. Conclusions It is my opinion that the Defendant’s warnings were not adequate since they 1) did not warn about risks associated with product use, 2) did not provide clear instructions for minimizing risks, 3) did not use language that was clear or understandable, and 4) did not use a format to optimally capture or hold attention. This is also reflected in how the Defendant’s warnings were designed. Specifically, in Mr. Mark Reilly’s deposition (personal capacity), Mr. Reilly agreed that there were no “scientific or warnings experts…involved in writing this [product] warning” and that the warning was written by an attorney (Page 9, lines 6-13). Based upon the materials reviewed, my education and experience, the manufacturers in this case knew or should have known that users could be exposed to a risk of significant injury or death under normal conditions of its use. The warnings provided did not reasonably inform an ordinary user of the nature and extent of the risk of death or serious health risks, such as those noted in the literature and discussed above, nor the means to avoid them. In the exercise of reasonable care, a manufacturer in similar industries should have included a warning that expressly described the risks of human consumption of kratom and the consequences of exposure. Meta-analyses show that well-designed warnings can educate people about product risks and change behavior to minimize risks. For instance, in a meta-analysis of tobacco warnings (the field for which we have the most evidence regarding the impact of substance use-related warnings), Noar et al. found that “pictorial warnings were more effective than text-only warnings for 12 of 17 effectiveness outcomes (all p<0.05).”13 Specifically, when examining different 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 239-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 40 outcomes, they found, “Relative to text-only warnings, pictorial warnings (1) attracted and held attention better; (2) garnered stronger cognitive and emotional reactions; (3) elicited more negative pack attitudes and negative smoking attitudes and (4) more effectively increased intentions to not start smoking and to quit smoking.”13 An example of an adequate warning related to dietary supplements is the FDA’s required warning on iron-containing dietary supplements. This warning states, “WARNING: Accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6. Keep this product out of reach of children. In case of accidental overdose, call a doctor or poison control center immediately.” This warning states the health risks associated with the product (“accidental overdose,” “fatal poisoning”), actions an individual can take to avoid risk (“keep this product out of reach of children,”), and actions an individual can take in case the risk occurs (“call a doctor or poison control center immediately”). In addition, the language used in the warning is clear, explicit, concise, and short. Finally, the warning is required to appear “prominently and conspicuously” and be placed on the actual product package (not a supplementary location). Had an adequate warning been given, it is more probable than not that ordinary, reasonable consumers would have altered their behavior—by not purchasing the product, not consuming the product, or changing their behavior in a way to mitigate risk and thereby have avoided injury or death. The burden of adding such a warning would have been minimal compared to the magnitude and likelihood of the harm. DEFENDANT’S MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO EXCLUDE PLAINTIFF’S EXPERT EVELYN CADMAN UNDER FED. RULE OF EVID. 702 Defendant JOpen, LLC (“Defendant” or “JOpen, LLC”) hereby files this Motion to Exclude Plaintiff’s Expert Witness Evelyn Cadman under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993) and incorporated memorandum of law. I. INTRODUCTION Plaintiff’s expert Evelyn Cadman does not offer scientific, toxicological, or industry-based opinions that would assist the jury in resolving any fact in dispute. Instead, her report advances a series of legal conclusions—that kratom is a “New Dietary Ingredient,” that O.P.M.S. products are “adulterated” and “misbranded,” and that Defendant violated federal regulatory law. These opinions exceed the proper scope of expert testimony under Rule 702 and Daubert for three independent reasons. First, Cadman lacks relevant expertise. She has no scientific, medical, or regulatory experience specific to kratom and admits she does not know which regulatory category kratom even falls into. Her opinions therefore rest on speculation outside her field of competence. 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 17 Second, Cadman repeatedly offers impermissible legal conclusions. She does not merely explain regulatory frameworks; she applies statutory terms of art such as “adulterated,” “misbranded,” “new drug,” and “new dietary ingredient” and declares that Defendant violated federal law. Courts uniformly prohibit experts from rendering such conclusions. Determining whether a product violates the FDCA is a legal question reserved for the Court. Third, even if her legal conclusions were permissible (they are not), they are unreliable because they rest on erroneous and unsupported assumptions about the Federal Food Drug and Cosmetic Act (FDCA)’s regulatory scheme. Her analysis collapses distinct statutory categories, ignores how products are classified based on labeling and marketing, and disregards regulatory realities reflected in the record. An opinion founded on an incorrect legal premise is not reliable under Rule 702. Because Cadman lacks relevant expertise, crosses the line into legal advocacy, and relies on faulty foundational assumptions, her testimony would confuse the jury rather than assist it. The Court should exclude her opinions in their entirety. II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND A. Plaintiff’s claims and allegations. This is a products liability case in which Plaintiff alleges that O.P.M.S. The district court has considerable discretion to admit or exclude expert testimony under Fed. R. Evi d . 702. See, Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 138–39 (1997); Seatrax, Inc. v. Sonbeck Int’l, Inc., 200 F.3d 358, 371 (5th Cir. 2000); Tajonera v. Black Elk Energy Offshore Operations, LLC, Civ. A. No. 13-0366, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8 (E.D. La. June 7, 2016) (Brown, J.) (citing authority). The burden rests with the party seeking to present the testimony to show that the requirements of Rule 702 are met. Moore v. Rule 702 provides that an expert witness “qualified ... by knowledge, skill, experience, training or education may testify in the form of an opinion” when the following requirements are met: (a) The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Rule 702 codifies the Supreme Court’s opinion in Daubert, which charges district courts to act as “gatekeeper” when determining the admissibility of expert testimony. Tajonera, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8. The purpose of a Daubert motion is “to ensure that only reliable and relevant expert testimony is presented to the jury.” Rushing v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 185 F.3d 496, 506 (5th Cir. 1999) (superseded by rule on other grounds) (citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 590–93). On appeal, courts “review the admission or exclusion of expert testimony for an abuse of discretion.” Braggs v. BP Expl. & Prod., Inc., No. 23-30297, 2024 WL 863356, at *2 (5th Cir. Feb. 29, 2024) (quoting Huss v. Gayden, 571 F.3d 442, 452 (5th Cir. 2009)). Courts “will not find error unless the ruling is manifestly erroneous.” Guy v. Crown Equip. Corp., 394 F.3d 320, 325 (5th Cir. 2004). This provides courts with “wide latitude in determining the admissibility of expert testimony.” Watkins v. Telsmith, Inc., 121 F.3d 984, 988 (5th Cir. 1997). B. The Court should exclude Cadman because her opinions are so fundamentally unsupported that they offer no assistance to the jury. 4

A court may exclude an expert’s testimony altogether if the opinions are substantially reliant on inappropriate legal opinions and lack factual support in the record, rendering the testimony fundamentally unreliable: [W]hile Daubert instructed that the focus of the reliability inquiry “must be solely on principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that they generate,” 509 U.S. at 595, 113 S. Ct. 2786, the Supreme Court later clarified that “conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct from one another,” Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 146, 118 S. Ct. 512, 139 L. Ed. 2d 508 (1997). Thus, “a district court’s focus on principles and methodology need not completely pretermit judicial consideration of an expert’s conclusions,” Kuhn, 686 F.3d at 625 (internal quotation marks omitted), and a district court may exclude expert testimony if it finds “that there is simply too great an analytical gap between the data and the opinion proffered,” Joiner, 522 U.S. at 146, 118 S.Ct. 512. Or, to put it in the language we have frequently used both before and after Daubert and Joiner, a district court may exclude an expert’s opinion if it is “so fundamentally unsupported” by its factual basis “that it can offer no assistance to the jury.” E.g., Loudermill v. Dow Chem. Co., 863 F.2d 566, 570 (8th Cir. 1988); United States v. Finch, 630 F.3d 1057, 1062 (8th Cir. 2011). In re Bair Hugger Forced Air Warming Devices Prods. Liab. Litig., 9 F.4th 768, 777–78 (8th Cir. 2021). If the factual basis of an expert’s opinion is so fundamentally unsupported because the expert fully relies on legal conclusions, altered facts and speculation, or fails to consider relevant facts in reaching a conclusion, the expert’s opinion can offer no assistance to the trier of fact, and is not admissible. E.g., Nebraska Plastics, Inc. v. Holland Colors Americas, Inc., 408 F.3d 410, 416–17 (8th Cir. 2005) (when opinion is “so fundamentally unsupported” in failure to consider relevant facts, it can offer no assistance to the trier of fact and must be excluded); McGlinchy v. Shell Chem. Co., 845 F.2d 802, 807 (9th Cir. 1988) (expert study and future testimony properly excluded where it rested on speculation, unsupported assumptions, and ignored distinctions crucial to arriving at a valid conclusion); Guillory v. Domtar Indus., Inc., 95 F.3d 1320, 1331 (5th Cir. 5

Cadman’s opinions rest on impermissible legal conclusions that are incorrect as a matter of law. a. Cadman’s opinions impermissibly cross the line into legal conclusions. Cadman’s report ultimately advances a single overarching conclusion: that Defendants’ products violated federal law. She opines that (1) kratom is a “New Dietary Ingredient” (“NDI”) under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act; (2) Defendants failed to submit a premarket NDI notification and the products are therefore “adulterated”; (3) the products were “misbranded”; (4) they were marketed as unapproved “new drugs”; and (5) the labels violated specific FDA regulatory provisions. See generally Ex. 1. In short, Cadman does not merely describe regulatory frameworks—she repeatedly concludes that Defendants violated them. Federal Rule of Evidence 704 permits testimony embracing an ultimate issue of fact, but it does not authorize experts to render legal conclusions. Courts have consistently drawn a careful distinction between (1) permissible testimony explaining complex regulatory schemes and industry practices, and (2) impermissible testimony opining that a party violated the law. See Snap- Drape, Inc. v. C.I.R., 98 F.3d 194, 198 (5th Cir. 1996) (Rule 704 “does not allow an expert to 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 8 of 17 render conclusions of law”); Commodores Ent. Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114, 1128–29 (11th Cir. 2018) (“the court must be the jury’s only source of law”). The governing line is well illustrated in Robinson v. Ethicon, Inc., 588 F. Supp. 3d 726 (S.D. Tex. 2022). There, the court permitted a regulatory expert to testify “about what the regulations require and [the company’s] conduct with regard to the regulations,” but held that the expert “cannot take the final step of opining that the product was ‘misbranded’ or ‘adulterated,’ as these are impermissible legal conclusions.” Id. at 736. That distinction is critical. Experts may explain regulatory standards; they may not apply statutory terms of art to reach ultimate legal determinations. See also In re Davol, Inc. Polypropylene Hernia Mesh Prods. Liab. Litig., 2021 WL 3286439, at *8 (S.D. Ohio Aug. 1, 2021) (prohibiting regulatory expert from offering opinion that product was “misbranded”). Cadman’s opinions repeatedly invoke precisely those legal terms of art. “Adulterated,” “misbranded,” “new dietary ingredient,” and “new drug” are not vernacular descriptors; they are statutory classifications defined by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and its implementing regulations. As the D.C. Circuit explained, when an expert “invok[es] a legal term of art,” the testimony “constitute[s] an impermissible legal conclusion.” Burkhart v. Washington Metro. Area Transit Auth., 112 F.3d 1207, 1213 (D.C. Cir. 1997). The proper inquiry is whether the terms “have a separate, distinct and specialized meaning in the law different from that present in the vernacular. If they do, exclusion is appropriate.” Id. at 1212 (quoting Torres v. County of Oakland, 758 F.2d 147, 151 (6th Cir. 1985)). The FDCA classifications at issue here unquestionably meet that standard. This is not a case where the expert simply describes regulatory background and leaves the ultimate question to the jury. Cadman goes further. She concludes that O.P.M.S. products “are 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 17 deemed adulterated,” “are misbranded,” “should not be sold as a drug,” and were marketed “in violation of [regulatory] standards.” Those statements are not technical explanations; they are legal determinations. Permitting such testimony would invert the jury’s role and the Court’s function. Whether a product is legally “adulterated,” “misbranded,” or an unlawful “new drug” under federal law is a question of statutory interpretation and legal application reserved for the Court. Allowing Cadman to supply those answers would improperly substitute expert opinion for judicial instruction. As courts have cautioned, they “must remain vigilant against the admission of legal conclusions.” Commodores, 879 F.3d at 1128–29. Cadman cannot opine that Defendant’s products violated those regulations or assign them statutory classifications that carry defined legal consequences. Her opinions that O.P.M.S. products were “adulterated,” “misbranded,” or unlawfully marketed therefore exceed the permissible scope of expert testimony and should be excluded. b. Cadman’s legal opinions are wrong and unsubstantiated. Cadman’s regulatory opinions all stem from her conclusions that (i) “Kratom is a New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) for purposes of the Dietary Supplement and Health Education Act of 1994” and (ii) “Defendants did not file a premarket NDI Notification and OPMS kratom is therefore deemed adulterated.” Ex. 1, at 3. Cadman’s conclusion is wrong. Of course the FDA is aware that O.P.M.S. is sold over the counter as a food and permits this even though the FDA has not issued any NDIN for O.P.M.S. This is because under the FDCA, whether a product is a “conventional food” or a “dietary supplement” depends on how it is labeled, packaged, and marketed to consumers. The FDCA has provisions that clearly distinguish between 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 17 foods, drugs, dietary supplements, and food additives. See 21 U.S.C. § 321(f). If it is not labeled, packaged, or marketed as a food supplement, the FDA regards it as a food. Cadman’s conclusions depend on a threshold legal assumption—that kratom must be treated as a “New Dietary Ingredient” requiring an NDI notification and that, absent such a notification, O.P.M.S. products are necessarily “adulterated.” That premise is simply wrong as a matter of federal law. Under the FDCA, whether a product is regulated as a conventional food, dietary supplement, drug, or food additive depends on how it is labeled, packaged, and marketed. See 21 U.S.C. § 321(f). A product not labeled or marketed as a dietary supplement is not automatically subject to the NDI framework. Cadman’s analysis collapses these distinct statutory categories and assumes that the absence of an NDIN renders the product unlawful—an assumption that does not reflect how the FDCA operates in practice. An expert opinion that rests on a false or legally erroneous premise is inadmissible under Rule 702. The Fifth Circuit has made clear that “the Daubert reliability analysis applies to, among other things, ‘the facts underlying the expert’s opinion.’” Jacked Up, LLC v. Sara Lee Corp., 291 F. Supp. 3d 795, 802 (N.D. Tex. 2018) (quoting Moore v. Int’l Paint, L.L.C., 547 F. App’x 513, 515 (5th Cir. 2013)). “In particular, an opinion based on ‘insufficient, erroneous information,’ fails the reliability standard.” Id. (quoting Paz v. Brush Engineered Materials, Inc., 555 F.3d 383, 389 (5th Cir. 2009)). Although Daubert is flexible, “the existence of sufficient facts … is in all instances mandatory.” Id. (quoting Hathaway v. Bazany, 507 F.3d 312, 318 (5th Cir. 2007)). Courts likewise recognize that while experts may incorporate legal assumptions into their analyses, “an expert’s reliance on incorrect legal assumptions would warrant exclusion.” Villalpando v. Exel Direct Inc., 161 F. Supp. 3d 873, 895 (N.D. Cal. 2016). Where the governing statutory framework contradicts the expert’s foundational premise, the testimony is unreliable. 10

My testimony and the conclusions reached in this report are and will be based on my education, training, and experience. A. OPMS Kratom: A New Dietary Ingredient Not Safe for Human Consumption. In the supplement industry, any entity looking to sell an ingredient or supplement for human consumption should first become familiar with the standards that govern the substance that is proposed for sale, including any agency guidance provided on the status of that substance. Kratom is a “New Dietary Ingredient” (NDI) for purposes of the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA). The FDA’s classification of kratom as an NDI is based upon the definitions established by Congress in DSHEA and is well publicized. See, for example, Import Alert 54-15 (FDA, 04/08/2021). The FDA has already established that kratom is an NDI. According to the publicly available Import Alert, to the best of the FDA’s knowledge, there is no information demonstrating that this substance was marketed as a dietary ingredient in the United States before October 15, 1994. See, Import Alert 54-15; see also, FDA letter to American Botanicals Corporation, dated Nov. 5, 2021. Because kratom is an NDI, any manufacturer or distributor proposing to sell kratom for human consumption should first familiarize themselves with the industry practices and standards that are necessary to confirm that the product is Page 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 31 reasonably expected to be safe. This standard of due diligence is also necessary for the premarket “NDI Notification” which must be submitted to the FDA at least 75 days before kratom can be introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce. Under this standard, the entity must substantiate a history of use or other evidence of safety establishing that the dietary ingredient, when used under the conditions recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement, will be reasonably be expected to be safe. If the required premarket NDI Notification does not acceptably demonstrate appropriate safety, then any dietary supplement product containing kratom is classified as an adulterated product, and not appropriate for sale to consumers because its safety has not been established. Based on the information provided, none of the named defendants ever verified that the OPMS kratom products manufactured and sold by them were reasonably safe for human consumption, either before or after they were marketed. FDA Response Letters to NDI Notifications pertaining to kratom uniformly confirm that the safety of kratom and its derivatives has not been established, and these products are not reasonably expected to be safe. Publicly available information from the FDA and elsewhere identify serious concerns regarding the toxicity of kratom in multiple organ systems, with risks to humans that include the risk of death. Food product labels do not instruct a consumer that the leafy material is to be used as a “botanical specimen”. Even if a kratom product were characterized and labeled as “food”, it would still need to be safe for human consumption. In fact, the safety standard for food ingredients places a higher burden on the industry than the standard for dietary ingredients in supplements. See, FDA – How U.S. FDA’s GRAS Notification Program Works (2/9/18) (https://www.fda.gov/food/generally-recognized-safe- gras/how-us-fdas-gras-notification-program-works). The GRAS standard Page 20

2/24/26, 3:25 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC DocumentFDA 241-4and Kratom | FiledFDA 03/02/26 Page 2 of 7 FDA and Kratom Kratom is a tropical tree (Mitragyna speciosa) that is native to Southeast Asia. Products prepared from kratom leaves are available in the U.S. online and in brick-and-mortar stores. Kratom is often used to self-treat conditions such as pain, coughing, diarrhea, anxiety and depression, opioid use disorder, and opioid withdrawal, with regular kratom users self-reporting using less than 6g of botanical kratom per consumption, per several recent (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7423016/) studies. An estimated 1.7 million Americans aged 12 and older used kratom in 2021, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s National Survey on Drug Use and Health Feedback (https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt39443/2021NSDUHFFRRev010323.pdf). Of note, 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) is a naturally occurring alkaloid in the kratom plant, but only a minor constituent that comprises less than 2% of the total alkaloid content in natural kratom leaves. However, 7-OH demonstrates substantially greater mu-opioid receptor potency than kratom’s primary alkaloid constituent mitragynine, as well as other classical opioids such as morphine. For more information about the agency’s efforts regarding 7-OH, see Hiding in Plain Sight: 7-OH Products (/news-events/public-health-focus/hiding-plain-sight-7-oh-products). There are no prescription or over-the-counter drug products containing kratom or its known alkaloids that are legally on the market in the U.S. If a new drug application (NDA) is submitted for kratom (or one of its components) to treat a specific medical condition, FDA will review the scientific data to determine if a drug product containing kratom (or its components) is safe and effective to treat that specific medical condition. Consistent with FDA’s practice with unapproved substances, until the agency scientists can evaluate the safety and effectiveness of kratom (or its components) in the treatment of any medical conditions, FDA will continue to warn the public against the use of kratom for medical treatment. The agency will also continue to monitor emerging data trends to better understand the substance and its components. https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-and-kratom 1/6

2/24/26, 3:25 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC DocumentFDA 241-4and Kratom | FiledFDA 03/02/26 Page 3 of 7 Kratom is not appropriate for use as a dietary supplement. FDA has concluded from available information, including scientific data, that kratom is a new dietary ingredient for which there is inadequate information to provide reasonable assurance that such ingredient does not present a significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury and, therefore, dietary supplements that are or contain kratom are adulterated under section 402(f)(1)(B) of the FD&C Act. Further, FDA has determined that kratom, when added to food, is an unsafe food additive within the meaning of section 409; food containing an unsafe food additive, such as kratom, is adulterated under section 402(a)(2)(C)(i). Based on these determinations by FDA, kratom is not lawfully marketed as a dietary supplement and cannot be lawfully added to conventional foods. Therefore, kratom is not lawfully marketed in the U.S. as a drug product, a dietary supplement, or a food additive in conventional food. What can happen if a person uses kratom? FDA has warned consumers not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder (SUD). In rare cases, deaths have been associated with kratom use, as confirmed by a medical examiner or toxicology reports. However, in these cases, kratom was usually used in combination with other drugs, and the contribution of kratom in the deaths is unclear. Cases of kratom-related SUD have also been observed. In these cases, individuals met certain criteria for SUD, including using kratom for longer than intended, using more kratom than intended, having cravings for kratom, continuing to use kratom despite adverse consequences (either physically or in their personal life), increasing the amount of kratom used to produce the same effect (tolerance), and experiencing withdrawal symptoms when kratom use was stopped (physical dependence). FDA is also aware of cases involving neonatal abstinence syndrome, in which newborns experienced withdrawal signs such as jitteriness, irritability, and muscle stiffness following prolonged exposure to kratom prior to birth. FDA has warned the public when certain kratom products were contaminated with Salmonella and/or concerning levels of heavy metals. These contaminants can put people at risk and can result in numerous documented illnesses. How is FDA protecting the public from the risks of kratom? https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-and-kratom 2/6

2/24/26, 3:25 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC DocumentFDA 241-4and Kratom | FiledFDA 03/02/26 Page 4 of 7 There are no FDA-approved kratom drug products or over-the-counter drugs containing kratom that are legally on the market in the U.S. FDA continues to warn consumers not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder (SUD). Consistent with its mission to protect the public’s health, FDA regularly exercises its authority to protect consumers from companies selling unapproved kratom drug products, making false or misleading claims about unproven benefits of kratom, and selling unlawfully marketed kratom dietary supplements and conventional foods. The agency has partnered with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection and with the Department of Justice to take numerous actions to limit the sale of unlawful kratom products in the U.S. The agency continues to work with its federal partners to warn the public about risks associated with use of kratom. Unapproved drug products are some of the most challenging products that FDA regulates, due to the complex and fragmented supply chain of distributors, wholesalers, retailers, and even individuals. These entities are not usually registered with FDA, may operate out of residences, and distribute kratom through sales made on the internet, social media, smoke/vape shops, other small stores, or by using the mail or other package delivery services. Kratom-containing drug products have been shipped through U.S. and international mail facilities and may falsely be declared as other items, such as potpourri or incense. FDA will continue to work with its federal partners to warn the public about the risks associated with the use of kratom and protect consumers from entities that are selling violative kratom products, including products with false or misleading labeling claims about unproven health benefits of kratom. Additionally, states may have their own regulations or prohibitions for kratom products. State health and law enforcement agencies are the best resource concerning applicable state laws. What is FDA doing to support sound scientific research on kratom? FDA recognizes that there is much that is not known scientifically about kratom. Although there are published animal studies with kratom extracts, there are few published reports from well-designed scientific studies where kratom was administered to humans. 2/24/26, 3:25 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC DocumentFDA 241-4and Kratom | FiledFDA 03/02/26 Page 5 of 7 investigation by researchers, including those in the academic community, drug companies, and government agencies, into the many safety issues and potential therapeutic uses of kratom would provide important public health information. What research is FDA doing on kratom? Research on Safety Issues While kratom contains over 50 alkaloids, most scientific research focuses on mitragynine and 7-OH, both of which bind to the same receptors in the brain (mu opioid receptors) as opioid drugs such as codeine. Mitragynine also has additional mechanisms of action on other chemical systems of the brain, including serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and kappa opioid receptors. These compounds may produce classic opioid-related effects such as sedation, nausea/vomiting, constipation, physical dependence/withdrawal, and respiratory depression that may lead to death. However, as with all drugs, the ability of kratom to cause harmful responses will depend on how much of the drug is taken and under what conditions. One additional safety concern with kratom is that of abuse potential. There are epidemiological data suggesting that some individuals develop substance use disorder following kratom use. To date, a well-designed human abuse potential study has not been conducted that would show whether kratom, mitragynine, or 7-OH produce rewarding effects (such as feeling “high”) that might lead an individual to abuse kratom. This means that the abuse potential of kratom has yet to be fully understood. Research on Kratom by FDA Clinical Investigators To better understand kratom’s safety profile, FDA funded a single ascending dose study to evaluate the effects of botanical kratom ingestion in humans. FDA researchers have submitted a manuscript to a peer-reviewed journal and will make the results publicly available upon acceptance. Building on this preliminary study, FDA awarded a grant for a human abuse potential study on kratom in September 2024. While these studies will further FDA’s efforts to characterize kratom’s safety profile, results from these studies will need to be considered in relation to the many and varied kratom-related products available to consumers and other scientific research. LEGAL STANDARD Under Rule 702, expert testimony is admissible only if the proponent establishes that, 1) the witness is qualified; 2) the testimony is reliable; and 3) the testimony will assist the trier of fact. The Court serves as gatekeeper to ensure that proposed expert testimony is both relevant and reliable. Daubert, 509 U.S. at 589; Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137 (1999). The central goal “is to ensure the reliability and relevancy of expert testimony.” Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., 509 U.S. 579, 589 (1993). Courts must evaluate qualification’s opinion by opinion, not in the abstract. Hall v. Flannery, 840 F.3d 922 (7th Cir. 2016). The focus, of course, must be solely on principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that they generate. Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 594–95 (1993). To qualify as “scientific knowledge,” an inference or assertion must be derived by the scientific method. Proposed testimony must be supported by appropriate validation—i.e., “good grounds,” based on what is known. In short, the requirement that an expert's testimony pertain to “scientific knowledge” establishes a standard of evidentiary reliability. Moore v. Ashland Chem. Inc., 151 F.3d 269, 274–75 (5th Cir. 1998) (Citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 589–90 (emphasis in original)) (internal citations omitted). A question of the validity of the methodology employed brings Daubert into play. MSOF Corporation v. Exxon Corporation, 2004–0988, p. 12 (La.App. 1st Cir.12/22/05), 934 So.2d 708, 718, writ denied, 2006–1669 (La.10/6/06), 938 So.2d 78. IV. Recognized methods of doing so include the differential diagnosis approach. Fifth Circuit precedent requires a two-step approach regarding medical opinions: proof of general causation and proof of specific causation. General causation asks whether the agent is capable of causing the injury. See e.g., Johnson v. Arkema, Inc., 685 F.3d 452, 468 (2012) (“General causation is whether a substance is capable of causing a particular injury or condition in the general population, while specific causation is whether a substance caused a particular individual's injury.”); Knight v. Kirby Inland Marine Inc., 482 F.3d 347, 351 (5th Cir. 2007) (Discussing the general and specific causation framework in a toxic tort case); Allen v. Pennsylvania Engineering Corp., 102 F.3d 194, (5th Cir. 1996); and Freeman v. Fon's Pest Management, Inc., 235 So.3d 1087 (2018). Specific causation requires a reliable method, such as differential etiology, linking the agent to the individual’s injury. “A differential diagnosis, properly performed, constitutes a reliable methodology for determining medical causation under Daubert.” In re Trasylol Prods. Liab. Litig.- MDL-1928, No. 08-MD-1928, 2013 WL 1192300, at *10 (S.D. Fla. Mar. 22, 2013) (Quoting Guinn v. Astrazeneca Pharms. LP, 602 F.3d 145, 153 (11th Cir.2010)). A differential diagnosis is a “patient-specific process of elimination that medical practitioners use to identify the most likely cause of a set of signs and symptoms from a list of possible causes.” Ruggiero v. Warner–Lambert Co., 424 F.3d 249, 254 (2d Cir.2005). It requires an expert to “determin[e] the possible causes for the patient's symptoms and then eliminat[e] each of the potential causes until reaching one that cannot be ruled out or determining which of those that cannot be excluded is the most likely.” Guinn, 602 F.3d at 1253 (quoting Westberry v. Gislaved Gummi AB, 178 F.3d 257, 262 (4th Cir.1999)). 4

Pure and highly concentrated caffeine products (/food/information-select-dietary-supplement-ingredients- and-other-substances/pure-and-highly-concentrated-caffeine) can have serious health consequences, including death. In the mid-2010s, pure or highly concentrated caffeine products emerged on the market. They were often marketed in bulk packaging with up to thousands of servings per container, which required consumers to measure out a safe serving from what can be a toxic or even lethal amount of bulk product. The FDA took action to protect consumers from these products. However, some products containing pure and highly concentrated caffeine remain on the market. Consumers should exercise caution when using such products. Signs of Consuming Too Much Caffeine Too much caffeine can cause a variety of symptoms: increased heart rate heart palpitations high blood pressure insomnia or sleep disruptions anxiety jitters upset stomach nausea headache Talk with your health care professional about your caffeine consumption if you have any of these symptoms. https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much 4/5

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 2 of 10 Overview What is a caffeine overdose? A caffeine overdose happens when you consume too much caffeine and it makes you sick. Healthcare providers sometimes call it caffeine toxicity. It’s a type of poisoning. Experts estimate that around 9 in 10 people in the U.S. have at least some caffeine every day. In small amounts, it has a stimulant effect — it can make you feel more awake, alert or like you have extra energy. For most people, it’s perfectly safe to enjoy a coffee, tea or soda. But there’s a limit to how much caffeine your body can take in and process at once. If you have more than what’s safe, you’ll experience symptoms that can damage your body. How much caffeine is too much? The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says that most adults can safely consume 400 milligrams of caffeine per day. That’s around two or three 12-ounce cups of coffee. The FDA doesn’t list a safe amount of caffeine for children. But experts say that kids younger than 2 shouldn’t have any caffeine. Children and teens should avoid highly caffeinated energy drinks. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 1/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 3 of 10 Everyone’s body responds differently to caffeine. Some people naturally have a higher tolerance to its effects than others. Certain health conditions and medications can make you more sensitive to its effects. Talk to a healthcare provider about how much caffeine is safe for you or your kids. They’ll give you a more specific amount based on your unique health. Symptoms and Causes Image content: This image is available to view online. View image online (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/-/scassets/images/org/health/articles/caffeine-overdose) You may experience overdose symptoms if you have an unsafe amount of caffeine. What are caffeine overdose symptoms? Caffeine overdose can cause lots of symptoms. You might notice any of these symptoms at first: Increased heart rate Feeling like your heart is racing (heart palpitations) Headache Anxiety Feeling jittery or agitated Increased peeing Increased thirst (polydipsia) Diarrhea https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 2/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 4 of 10 Trouble sleeping Symptoms of a more serious overdose include: Trouble breathing or shortness of breath (dyspnea) Sudden high blood pressure (hypertension) Muscle twitching Confusion Nausea and vomiting Seizures What causes a caffeine overdose? Consuming too much caffeine causes a caffeine overdose. Caffeine occurs naturally in some plants. It can also be a human-made chemical added to foods, drinks, medications and supplements. You can probably guess some of the most well-known caffeinated drinks, including: Coffee Tea Soda Hot chocolate Energy drinks Manufacturers also add caffeine to lots of other products (including some you may not think of), including: Protein bars and pre- or post-workout snacks https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 3/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 5 of 10 Sports or exercise recovery drinks Over-the-counter (OTC) medications like some decongestants and pain relievers Energy supplements advertised to help keep you awake (caffeine pills) OTC diet pills or appetite suppressants Chewing gum It’s more common for people to experience a caffeine overdose from supplements mixing highly caffeinated drinks with medication. But no matter where it comes from, if you ingest too much caffeine, your body can’t process it fast enough and you may have an overdose. What are caffeine overdose complications? Severe complications of a caffeine overdose are rare, but can include: Low potassium in your blood (hypokalemia) High blood sugar (hyperglycemia) Too much acid in your blood (metabolic acidosis) Kidney damage Brain damage Heart damage Diagnosis and Tests How do healthcare providers diagnose a caffeine overdose? https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 4/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 6 of 10 A healthcare provider will diagnose a caffeine overdose with a physical exam and some tests. They might do a neurological exam. They’ll ask about your symptoms and when they first started. Tell your provider anything you’ve drank, eaten or taken that has caffeine in it (and how much or how many you had). Your provider will use blood tests to check for caffeine and/or higher levels of acid that mean your body is breaking down and processing it. They may also do a urinalysis to check your pee. You might need an EKG or chest X- ray, too, to see how your heart is working. Management and Treatment How do you treat a caffeine overdose? Your provider will suggest treatments to manage any symptoms you’re experiencing and help your body process the caffeine as safely as possible. What you’ll need will depend on how much caffeine you’ve had and how it’s affecting you. You might not need any specific treatment. Your provider may suggest drinking water to stay hydrated and keeping an eye on any changes in your body. If you do need treatment, your provider may use: Intravenous (IV) fluids for hydration Medications to stabilize your blood pressure Activated charcoal to help your body process the caffeine Dialysis to support your kidneys https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 5/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 7 of 10 Defibrillation to restore your normal heart rate You might need other medications or treatments for specific symptoms. Your provider will tell you what to expect. Outlook / Prognosis How long do caffeine overdose symptoms last? How long a caffeine overdose lasts depends on its severity and how much excess caffeine you had. Caffeine usually takes three to 10 hours to break down in our bodies. But an overdose can last longer than that because your stomach absorbs caffeine very quickly when you first ingest it. Some factors that can affect how long you experience symptoms include your: Age Weight Natural caffeine tolerance Your healthcare provider will tell you what to expect and which signs of any complications to watch out for. They’ll tell you when it’s safe to return to eating and drinking normally and if it’s safe to have caffeine again. Can you die from a caffeine overdose? It’s rare, but a caffeine overdose can be fatal. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 6/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 8 of 10 Even if you don’t experience an overdose, regularly having unsafe levels of caffeine can damage your heart and central nervous system. Prevention Can you prevent a caffeine overdose? Consuming only a safe amount of caffeine each day is the best way to avoid a caffeine overdose. That might sound obvious, but lots of foods and drinks may have more caffeine in them than you realize. Check the nutrition and ingredient labels on items to see if they contain caffeine (and how much). The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) keeps a searchable database that shows how much caffeine is in foods and drinks. Help kids and teens understand the risks of having too much caffeine, and help your family make safe choices. Talk to a healthcare provider about how much caffeine is safe for you and your children. Living With When should I seek care for a caffeine overdose? Get medical attention as soon as you think you’re having any symptoms of a caffeine overdose — especially if you know you’ve had a lot of caffeine. Go to the emergency room or call 911 (or your local emergency services number). https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/caffeine-overdose 7/9

2/22/26, 7:09 PMCase 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC CaffeineDocumentOverdose: 249-12Symptoms, TreatmentFiled& Side03/02/26Effects Page 9 of 10 In the U.S., you can also call the national Poison Help hotline at 1.800.222.1222. An expert will tell you what you should do and how to stay safe while you’re waiting to get treatment. Don’t try to treat a caffeine overdose at home. Never make yourself or someone else vomit unless a poison control expert or healthcare provider tells you to. Which questions should I ask my healthcare provider? Which treatments will I need? How long will it take me to recover? Is it safe for me to have caffeine again in the future? Which foods, drinks, medicines or supplements should I avoid? A note from Cleveland Clinic Everyone who drinks coffee or tea knows that pleasant extra zip can help you get through a long day. And using caffeine (even regularly) can be completely safe. But you might be having more caffeine every day than you realize. Keep an eye on how much you’re having, and talk to a healthcare provider about how much caffeine is safe for you to use. It usually takes a large amount of caffeine to cause an overdose, but it can cause some serious symptoms. Get medical help or call a poison control center right away if you think you’re experiencing a caffeine overdose. Medically Reviewed.
