The neurobehavioral effects of kratom are more subtle than the commonly described stimulant effects at low doses and opioid effects at higher doses. Low doses of kratom increase alertness, energy, and talkativeness. At doses greater than 5 grams, however, kratom users describe the persistence of heightened alertness coupled with analgesia. These effects account for the use of kratom as a mild stimulant for manual laborers, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. 20. Some of the biological effects of kratom arise from binding of alkaloidal components to a number of neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system, including the µ-opioid (MOR), κ-opioid, serotonergic (5-HT), and alpha (α1) receptors, among others. MOR activity is particularly important. MOR activation mediates pain, respiratory rate, gastrointestinal transit time, nausea, and pruritis, among other effects. Each of these effects is mediated via distinct signaling pathways following binding of an agonist to the MOR receptor. 21. Classical opioid agonists (e.g., morphine and fentanyl) are “unbiased” agonists in that they indiscriminately activate all biological effects mediated by MOR. Kratom is different. The most prevalent—and best studied—alkaloid in kratom is mitragynine. In contrast to classical unbiased MOR agonists, mitragynine is a “biased” agonist in that it produces some, but not all, effects that arise from receptor binding of a classical MOR agonist such as morphine or fentanyl. 22. For example, while mitragynine produces analgesia, it does not produce the stupor characteristic of classic, unbiased MOR agonists. Instead, kratom produces increased alertness. Furthermore, mitragynine does not produce the respiratory depression that is a leading cause of mortality from classical unbiased MOR agonist overdose (Macko 1972; Varadi 2016; Kruegel 2019; Boyer 2012). 23. In fact, the clinical features as well as the time course of the toxidrome from kratom has never been described. Testing for mitragynine is generally limited to commercial forensic companies and medical examiner offices. Mitragynine itself undergoes postmortem redistribution; the postmortem concentration of mitragynine measured by forensic laboratories is over three times higher than premortem blood. 24. In fact, the FDA in its recent report entitled “7- Hydroxymitragynine (7-OH): An Assessment of the Scientific Data and Toxicological Concerns Around an Emerging Opioid Threat” declined to even analyze FAERS data because of the striking limitations of the database. (https://www.fda.gov/files/drugs/published/7-hydroxymitragynin_7- oh_an_assessment_of_the_scientific_data_and_toxicological_concerns_around_an_emerging_op ioid_threat.pdf). 2 The QT interval is a measure of cardiac repolarization on the electrocardiogram that has been associated with a specific type of ventricular dysrhythmia known as Torsades de Pointes (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21915-torsades-de- pointeshttps://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21915-torsades-de-pointes). 3 No cardiac rhythm was described in the case report, only that the patient was “pulseless” (Abdullah 2019). 14

Dr. Williams also claims there are “significant drug-drug interactions involving MG and 7HMG,” but he cannot point to any scientifically sound example where kratom or its alkaloids led to any pharmacodynamic interactions between kratom, its alkaloids, and other drugs. Rebuttal to Josef Thundiyil’s report 98. I have reviewed the report of Dr. Thundiyil. Dr. Thundiyil disagrees with both the medical examiner and cardiac pathologists, disregarding important autopsy findings that inform the cause of death. For example, he reports the high origin of the left coronary artery, but he disregards the acute angle of origin and its recognized association with sudden cardiac death. Similarly, Dr. Thundiyil ignores entirely the anatomic flap that obscures the origin of the artery. Any anatomic feature that obstructs blood flow into an artery is likely to produce end organ damage. Depending on the location of the obstruction (e.g., near the takeoff of a major artery) and the organ that artery perfuses (e.g., the heart), death is a likely outcome—exactly as recognized by several publication in the medical literature (Rizzo 2021; Taylor 1992; Muriago 1997; Loukas 2016; Virmani 1984; Nishida 2014). 99. Dr. Thundiyil incorrectly states that a mitragynine blood concentration of 150 ng/mL is sufficient to be lethal. First, a blood concentration of 150 ng/mL is within the range of concentrations achieved in clinical trials where no adverse events occurred (Heustis 2024). Second, Dr Thundiyil disregards the known postmortem redistribution of mitragynine. Based on the existing literature, Ms. Moller’s likely premortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately 50 ng/mL (Osawa 2025). 100. Dr. Thundiyil recognizes the presence of caffeine as identified by the medical examiner, but he misses that the methylxanthine toxidrome could be present. Dr. Thundiyil also overlooks Ms. Moller’s use of multiple dietary supplements that contained caffeine and other vasoactive compounds for which there is evidence of use. Furthermore, Harmony Moller exhibited a well-recognized toxidrome of protracted vomiting unresponsive to antiemetics, had no anatomic cause of death other than her congenital heart disease that is known to be lethal by itself, and had a qualitative caffeine measurement. 101. Dr. Thundiyil correctly disagrees with Dr. Williams that neither diphenhydramine nor promethazine contributed to Ms. Moller’s death. As no pharmacodynamic interactions have plausibly been attributed to kratom use, the likelihood that one arose now, particularly involving multiple medications with minimal cardiovascular effects at such low concentrations, is low. 102. I am able to defend rigorously these conclusions, made within a reasonable degree of medical and toxicologic certainty. I reserve the right to supplement, amend or addend these opinions based on additional or new information including other expert reports. 15

LEGAL STANDARD “The court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56. Materiality is a matter of substantive law, and “[o]nly disputes over facts that might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law will properly preclude the entry of summary judgment. Factual disputes that are irrelevant or unnecessary will not be counted.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). “A fact is considered material when its existence or nonexistence may be essential to plaintiff’s cause of action under the applicable theory of recovery.” Smith v. Our Lady of the Lake Hospital, Inc., 639 So. 2d 730, 751 (La. 1994). “A genuine issue is one about which reasonable persons could disagree.” Hines v. Garrett, 876 So. 2d 764, 765 (La. 2004). In determining whether a genuine issue of material fact exists, the court must view all evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party. Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372, 380 (2007). The party asserting that a material fact “cannot be or is genuinely disputed” must support the assertion by either: (1) citing to particular parts of materials in the record, including depositions, documents, electronically stored information, affidavits or declarations, stipulations (including 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 4 of 12 those made for purposes of the motion only), admissions, interrogatory answers, or other materials; or (2) showing that the materials cited do not establish the absence or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot produce admissible evidence to support the fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(1)(A)–(B). If the moving party has carried its burden, the non-movant must “come forward with ‘specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.’” Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986). The nonmoving party, however, cannot satisfy his summary judgment burden with conclusory allegations, unsubstantiated assertions, or only a scintilla of evidence. Little v. Liquid Air Corp., 37 F.3d 1069, 1075 (5th Cir. 1994) (en banc). “One of the principal purposes of the summary judgment rule is to isolate and dispose of factually unsupported claims or defenses[.]” Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323–24 (1986). If a party bears the burden of proof “to establish the existence of an element essential to that party’s case,” but fails to make a sufficient showing, “Rule 56(c) mandates the entry of summary judgment” against the party. Id. at 322. Under Louisiana law, fault may only be allocated where there is evidence of negligent conduct that was a legal cause of the harm. La. C.C. Art. 2323. Defendants cannot establish such a standard of care when their packaging and disclaimers fail to state any risk of kratom use associated to cardiac conditions and fail to state any risk of death whatsoever.2 Comparative fault is not appropriate where: 2 There can be no assumption of risk in this matter as well. Co., 469 So.2d 967 (La. 1985) (explaining that comparative fault requires unreasonable conduct). III. UNDISPUTED MATERIAL FACTS The following facts are undisputed: 1. Harmony Moller ingested OPMS Green Vein Maeng Da Silver kratom capsules and powder. 2. The product was manufactured, marketed, and sold by Defendants. 3. The product label did not warn of risk of sudden death, risk of fatal toxicity, any lethal dosing threshold, drug-drug interactions, or adverse cardiac risks. 4. There is no evidence that Harmony altered the product, used it in a manner inconsistent with its intended purpose; or ignored any warning. IV. ARGUMENT A. A consumer cannot be comparatively at fault for failing to heed to warnings that do not exist. Under Louisiana law, failure to warn liability turns on whether the manufacturer provided adequate warnings regarding known or reasonably known risks. (See L.P.L.A. 9:2800.54 (B)(3), see also, Marks v. OHMEDA, Inc., 871 So.2d 1148, 2003-1446 (La.App. 3 Cir. 3/31/04)(“A product is unreasonably dangerous because an adequate warning about the product has not been provided if, at the time the product left its manufacturer’s control, the product possessed a characteristic that may cause damage and the manufacturer failed to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning of such characteristic and its danger to users and handlers of the product.”) 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 12 Where no warning exists, a consumer cannot be comparatively at fault for failing to avoid an undisclosed danger. Comparative fault requires some negligent act or omission by the plaintiff. La. C.C. art. 2323. A consumer cannot be negligent for failing to avoid a risk that was never disclosed. The undisputed evidence establishes that the OPMS kratom product consumed by Harmony Moller contained no warnings that the product could cause serious cardiovascular effects or death. See photos of the products Harmony consumed, attached as Exhibits 1 & 2. The labels likewise provided no dosing instructions, maximum use guidance, instructions for safe consumption, warnings regarding drug-drug interactions, risk of death, or risk of cardiac adverse events. Id. The death certificate and autopsy report conclude that Harmony died as a result of abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine use. Autopsy Report, attached as Exhibit 3. The very mechanism of harm involves a pharmacological risk associated with kratom consumption. Precisely the type of risk that would require an adequate warning. Defendants and their own experts acknowledge that kratom consumption is associated with significant adverse effects, including death. In his report, Dr. Jack Henningfield cites to NIDA materials stating that “deaths have been linked to kratom products.” See Henningfield’s report, attached as Exhibit 4 at pg. 13. He further identifies numerous adverse effects associated with kratom use, including addiction, psychotic symptoms, tachycardia, seizures, hepatotoxicity, and other serious health consequences. Id. Yet none of these risks appear on the OPMS product label. Defendants’ corporate representatives concede the importance of warning consumers of known risks. On October 8, 2025, Mark Reilly, owner of the OPMS trademark, testified in his individual capacity that manufacturers selling products for human consumption should 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 12 communicate instructions for safe use and disclose significant health risks, including a risk of death if one exists. See Excerpt from Reilly’s Deposition, attached as Exhibit 5 at 32:1–23. Similarly, JOpen, LLC, the distributor of OPMS kratom products, testified that products should include warnings regarding known risks and that companies should stay current with scientific and medical research concerning kratom’s safety. See Excerpt from JOpen’s Deposition, attached as Exhibit 6 at 29:15–25. Defendant Mark Jennings further acknowledged that if kratom adversely affects the cardiovascular system, that risk should be disclosed to consumers. See Excerpt from Jennings’ Deposition, attached as Exhibit 7 at 46–47. Defendants’ experts focus on Harmony’s underlying, and unknown to her, cardiac condition. Exhibits 4, 11 – 14. Given the condition was unknown and Defendants’ failure to warn of any cardiac risk for kratom, Harmony’s underlying cardiac condition cannot and should not be used as a factor for placing blame upon Harmony. Exhibits 1 & 2. Such evidence would only invite the trier of fact to speculate without an appropriate factual basis. Notably, although the OPMS label contains no such warnings, the disclaimer on the OPMS website, which is controlled by JOpen, acknowledges serious potential side effects associated with kratom, including seizures, liver damage, addiction, withdrawal, abuse, and death. See Website Disclaimer, attached as Exhibit 8, see Exhibit 6, 111: 23 – 24. This admission underscores Defendants’ awareness of serious risks while simultaneously failing to warn consumers. Since no warning regarding cardiovascular risk or death appeared on the product Harmony consumed, she cannot, as a matter of law, be comparatively at fault for failing to heed a warning that was never given. 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 8 of 12 B. There is no evidence that Harmony Moller misused the product. Comparative fault also fails because there is no evidence that Harmony misused the OPMS product. Kratom ingestion was the precise purpose for which Defendants manufactured, marketed, and sold OPMS kratom. Defendants testified that they themselves have used kratom, in various forms, and the OPMS kratom package suggests that the manufacturers and sellers of the product and intend for it to be consumed. Exhibits 1, 2, and Exhibit 6 at 92:1–21. 1) Defendants sold OPMS kratom for human consumption, in other words, they knew consumers would ingest their products. a. Exhibit 9 (Martian Deposition) at 97:19 - 22 & Exhibit 5 (Reilly Deposition) at 37:2-12 b. Exhibit 10, JOPEN RFA, No. 9. There is no evidence in the record that Harmony consumed the product in an abnormal, reckless, or unforeseeable manner. Moreover, the record contains no evidence that she ingested an unusual or excessive quantity. (See, LSA-R.S. 9:2800.5, stating that, “even when product misuse occurred, manufacturer was still required to give adequate warnings if misuse was reasonably foreseeable.”) Indeed, multiple experts opine that the level of mitragynine in Harmony Moller’s system was low. See Reports drafted by Boyer, McCurdy, Huestis, and Paustenbach, attached as Exhibits 11 - 14. Where a product is sold for ingestion, provides no dosing guidance, and carries no warnings of serious health risks, a consumer’s ordinary use of that product cannot constitute misuse or comparative fault. C. Speculation regarding other substances cannot create comparative fault. 8

However, neither the death certificate nor the autopsy attributes death to these medications. Id. Defense experts have also focused on photos of Harmony’s room at the time of her passing, speculating and insinuating that substances found in her room, but not in her system at the of death, somehow played a role in her death. Exhibits 11, 13 – 14. There is no support for such a speculative and baseless proposition. For instance, Dr. Boyer, Dr. Huestis, Dr. Paustenbach, and Dr. McCurdy all mention the presence of diet pills and prescription pill bottles in Harmony’s room, yet none of the substances they reference are present in the operative toxicology report. In short, to the extent any evidence of Harmony’s use of dietary supplements and the presence of other medications or alcohol in her room are entered into evidence (which they should not be pursuant to Plaintiff’s simultaneously filed motion in limine for exclusion of evidence, incorporated herein by reference)3, such evidence should not be considered in relation to any claim for comparative negligence as there no record evidence that any such substances were used by Harmony preceding her death, as they are not in the relevant toxicology report. Absent expert testimony establishing causation, the mere presence of commonly used antihistamine and anti-emetic medications cannot create a triable issue of fact for comparative fault. Speculation regarding polypharmacy cannot defeat summary judgment. D. Comparative fault will improperly undermine the purpose of the eggshell plaintiff rule. See Lasha v. Olin Corp., 625 So.2d 1002, 1003 (La. 1993) (“a defendant takes his victim as he finds him; when the defendant's tortious conduct aggravates a pre-existing injury or condition, he must compensate the victim for the full extent of this aggravation”); see also, Louisiana Civil Code Article 2315 (Stating “every act whatever of man that causes damage to another obliges him by whose fault it happened to repair it.”) The court in Lasha, emphasized that “the defendant's liability for damages is not mitigated by the fact that the plaintiff's pre-existing physical infirmity was responsible in part for the consequences of the plaintiff's injury by the defendant.” Lasha v. Olin Corp., 625 So.2d 1002, 1005 (LA. 1993). In Latulippe v. Braun, the court stated “it is well-settled that a tortfeasor takes his victim as he finds him and when a defendant's tortious conduct aggravates a pre-existing condition, the defendant must compensate the victim for the full extent of the aggravation.” Latulippe v. Braun, 18-83 (La. App. 5 Cir. 8/10/18), 253 So. 3d 820, 833 (citing, Maranto v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., 94-2603 and 94-2615, p. 3 (La. 2/20/95), 650 So.2d 757, 759.) Federal courts applying Louisiana law in diversity cases consistently recognize and apply Louisiana's eggshell plaintiff doctrine. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals addressed the doctrine's application under federal diversity jurisdiction in Dahlen v. Gulf Crews, Inc., confirming that Louisiana's eggshell skull doctrine “requires a defendant to compensate a plaintiff for unforeseeable injuries flowing from some pre-existing physical condition.” Dahlen v. Gulf Crews, Inc., 281 F.3d 487, 495 (5th Cir. 2002) (Finding Louisiana's doctrine consistent with federal law and the Restatement (Second) of Torts § 461); see also, Koch v. United States, 857 F.3d 267, 274 (5th Cir. 2017) (“this court and district courts within our circuit have expressed approval and 10

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 11 of 12 acceptance of the ‘thin skull,’ ‘eggshell skull,’ or ‘defendant takes the victim as found’ rule without limiting its application to latent or unmanifested preexisting conditions”). Notably this is exactly such an eggshell skull case, as the St. Tammany Parish Coroner’s office, via medical examiner, Dr. Defatta, determined the cause of Harmony’s death was left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine [kratom] (emphasis added). Exhibit 3. Further every proposed expert has opined that Harmony’s cardiac condition played a role in her death, recognizing the important role of Harmony’s eggshell status due to her underlying cardiac condition. Exhibits 11 - 14. In short, any argument of comparative fault based upon Harmony’s underlying cardiac condition, failure to follow packaging instructions or warnings, and the photos, videos, and evidence of substances in her room at time of death cannot be used to support a claim of comparative fault as there is no genuine issue of fact regarding such a claim. V. CONCLUSION For the foregoing reasons, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court grant partial summary judgment dismissing any affirmative defense alleging comparative fault of decedent Harmony Moller and precluding Defendants from presenting such argument at trial. Kratom (Mitragynia speciosa Korth) is a tree-like plant native to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and other parts of southeast Asia. Indigenous users create a “juice” by boiling fresh kratom leaves for several hours that is then diluted with hot water to make kratom tea. Kratom is used in traditional environments to treat diarrhea, hypertension, cough, fever, impotence, and other ailments. Kratom is used by manual laborers for its mild stimulant effects, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. In the west, many different kratom formulations are available, including tinctures, extracts, capsules, softgels, concentrated products, as well as dried leaf powders and cut leaf material. 5

December 18, 2025 Page 6 Kratom in western countries is most commonly used as a remedy for opioid addiction, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. 19. The neurobehavioral effects of kratom are more subtle than the commonly described stimulant effects at low doses and opioid effects at higher doses. Low doses of kratom increase alertness, energy, and talkativeness. At doses greater than 5 grams, however, kratom users describe the persistence of heightened alertness coupled with analgesia. These effects account for the use of kratom as a mild stimulant for manual laborers, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. 20. Some of the biological effects of kratom arise from binding of alkaloidal components to a number of neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system, including the µ-opioid (MOR), κ-opioid, serotonergic (5-HT), and alpha (α1) receptors, among others. MOR activity is particularly important. MOR activation mediates pain, respiratory rate, gastrointestinal transit time, nausea, and pruritis, among other effects. Each of these effects is mediated via distinct signaling pathways following binding of an agonist to the MOR receptor. 21. Classical opioid agonists (e.g., morphine and fentanyl) are “unbiased” agonists in that they indiscriminately activate all biological effects mediated by MOR. Kratom is different. The most prevalent—and best studied—alkaloid in kratom is mitragynine. In contrast to classical unbiased MOR agonists, mitragynine is a “biased” agonist in that it produces some, but not all, effects that arise from receptor binding of a classical MOR agonist such as morphine or fentanyl. 22. For example, while mitragynine produces analgesia, it does not produce the stupor characteristic of classic, unbiased MOR agonists. Instead, kratom produces increased alertness. Furthermore, mitragynine does not produce the respiratory depression that is a leading cause of mortality from classical unbiased MOR agonist overdose (Macko 1972; Varadi 2016; Kruegel 2019; Boyer 2012). 23. In fact, the clinical features as well as the time course of the toxidrome from kratom has never been described. Testing for mitragynine is generally limited to commercial forensic companies and medical examiner offices. Mitragynine itself undergoes postmortem redistribution; the postmortem concentration of mitragynine measured by forensic laboratories is over three times higher than premortem blood. 24. In general, adverse events attributed to kratom have been derived from database studies, poorly controlled case reports, or small case series, each of which has serious deficiencies in patient background information, including medical, social, or family history; clinical evaluation; scene findings; or analytical technique. These poorly controlled studies at times associate kratom with agitation, seizures, liver injury, renal injury, ventricular dysrhythmia, and respiratory depression. Individually and collectively, these studies lack the scientific heft to establish causation between kratom use and any adverse event. 25. For example, case reports describing right ventricular failure in the setting of intermittent kratom ingestions are complicated by the distant use of kratom, the lack of clarity 6
